slides.title: Case Management Training — Day 2
slides.notes: Welcome to Day 2 of Case Management Training with Legal Support Help. Yesterday we carried a case from intake through the Treatment Phase. Today we follow it to the money: how we audit the file before the demand, how we build and send the Bodily Injury demand, and how we negotiate and close the settlement. Keep John Doe's file in mind as we go, because every phase today comes back to it.

slides.title: Training Agenda
slides.notes: Here is our agenda for today, in three parts. Part one: the Pre-Demand phase, where we audit the whole file before anything goes to the adjuster. Part two: the Bodily Injury Demand, where we build the demand packet and present the case. Part three: the BI Settlement, where we negotiate, finalize the paperwork, and move the file from settled to paid.

slides.title: Pre-Demand Case Auditing: Core Objectives
slides.notes: Pre-demand case auditing, often called a Forensic Case Audit or a Pre-Litigation Audit, is the rigorous process of vetting a claim's evidence and value before a formal demand letter goes out. It has four core objectives. Verification: do the facts in the demand letter match the physical evidence, for example, do the photos of the crash match the police report? Valuation: are the damages calculated accurately, with the medical bills, lost wages, and future care costs audited so every expense is justified? Risk assessment: where are the weak spots where the defense may argue comparative negligence, meaning partial fault on the client's part? And compliance: does the case meet statutory requirements, like the Statute of Limitations, before the demand is issued? The audit is a sanity check that makes the claim bulletproof.

slides.title: The Auditing Checklist: The Trinity of Case Alignment
slides.notes: The goal of this audit is simple: when the demand letter lands on an adjuster's desk, there are zero easy outs for the defense. A successful audit keeps three pillars perfectly synchronized. The Narrative: the client's story of how the incident happened. The Physicality: the property damage, and the biomechanics, meaning the force of the impact. And the Medicals: the clinical proof of injury. If one pillar is out of alignment, the case value collapses. So the audit question is this: do the property damage photos support the mechanism of injury described in the medical records? A full pre-demand audit is the final stress test of a file. It is the move from collecting information to weaponizing it.

slides.title: Master Audit Checklist: Financial & Lien Verification
slides.notes: The Master Audit Checklist starts with financial and lien verification. This is the math portion of the audit. Special damages are the sum of all medical bills, plus property damage, plus lost wages. For lost wages, make sure you have a signed letter from the employer and a disability slip from the doctor. Without both, adjusters usually reject the lost wage claim. Then lien resolution: identify every subrogation interest, both statutory, like Medicare, Medicaid, ERISA, and the VA, and consensual, like medical provider liens under LOPs. Mistakes here lead to short-funded settlements where the client takes home nothing.

slides.title: Master Audit Checklist: Liability Proof
slides.notes: Next on the checklist is liability proof. For the police or incident report, verify the final version, not just the exchange of information, and check it for citations or contributory negligence notes. For witness statements, confirm the contact information is still valid, and audit for statement drift: did the witness's story change? Then the scene audit: review Google Earth or dashcam footage to make sure the physics of the claim are possible.

slides.title: Master Audit Checklist: Property Damage Deep Dive
slides.notes: Third, the property damage deep dive. Audit the photos for a clear point of impact. Are there photos of the undercarriage or the frame? Those are crucial in high-value injury claims. Compare the insurance estimate with the final body shop bill, and look for supplementals that prove hidden structural damage. And if the vehicle was totaled, verify the CCC One or other valuation report, and make sure the client is not being lowballed on the value of the vehicle.

slides.title: Master Audit Checklist: Medical & Billing Audit
slides.notes: Fourth, the medical and billing audit. Build a chronology, a timeline of treatment, and audit it for gaps in treatment. If there is a 14-day gap, you must have a documented reason, for example, the client was waiting for MRI authorization. Run a coding audit: scan the bills for unbundling or duplicate CPT codes that could make a bill look inflated, or even fraudulent, to an adjuster. And review the client's prior history, the past 5–10 years of medical records, so you find any pre-existing conditions before the defense does.

slides.title: The Defense-Eye Audit: Red Flag Detection
slides.notes: Before finalizing the demand, audit the file the way the defense will, for these value killers. Social media presence: if the client claims loss of enjoyment of life but posted vacation photos during treatment, adjust the demand or warn the client. MIST designation: if the property damage is under one to two thousand dollars, the case is classified as Minor Impact Soft Tissue, so provide stronger medical narratives to counter the bias that low damage means no injury. And the venue audit: confirm where a suit would be filed, and whether the jury pool is conservative or liberal, because that affects the multiplier for pain and suffering.

slides.title: Final Package Readiness
slides.notes: An audited file is organized for the attorney's final review in three parts. A summary memo: a one-page cheat sheet of the audit findings. An exhibit index: all bills, records, and property damage photos, labeled. And the Ask: a calculated demand range, based on the policy limits and the total specials. A pro tip: always audit the policy limits one last time. There is nothing worse than sending a one hundred thousand dollar demand, only to learn mid-negotiation that the defendant has a twenty-five thousand dollar step-down policy.

slides.title: Case Phase: Demand — The Legal & Procedural Foundation
slides.notes: Now we move into the Demand phase. Bodily Injury demand workflows bring together legal expertise, medical understanding, and negotiation skills. Case Managers must understand the why behind the paperwork, and that rests on three foundations: the Statute of Limitations, the liability framework, and the coverage analysis. Your job is to progress cases efficiently from intake to disbursement, meeting every deadline and identifying the key value drivers.

slides.title: Case Phase: Demand — The Policy Limit Mindset
slides.notes: In this phase, a Case Manager shifts from a reactive mindset to a proactive, strategic one. It is all about identifying needs, quantifying requirements, and setting the stage. Think in terms of the policy limit mindset. The goal is not just to send a packet of records. It is to present the case in a way that makes the insurance adjuster afraid of a jury. Two checks come first. Maximum Medical Improvement, or MMI: make sure the client has completed treatment, or has a clear future care plan. And the gap check: identify and explain any gaps in treatment before the adjuster uses them to devalue the case.

slides.title: Treatment Gaps in the Demand Phase
slides.notes: Let's look closer at treatment gaps. Adjusters use them to argue that the injuries were not serious, that the treatment was unnecessary or excessive, that the client recovered earlier than claimed, or that other unrelated factors caused the condition. Unexplained gaps can reduce settlement value. So the Case Manager's strategy is to identify gaps early during record review, document the reason for every interruption in treatment, obtain supporting documents when available, and include the explanations directly in the demand package timeline. When you address a gap in the demand, acknowledge it clearly, give the context and supporting facts, connect continued symptoms to ongoing treatment, and show the complaints were consistent before and after the gap. A well-explained treatment gap is less damaging than an unexplained one.

slides.title: The Demand Packet Checklist
slides.notes: Before the attorney reviews the demand letter, the Case Manager makes sure the Big Four components are flawless. Medical specials: a clean, itemized spreadsheet of every provider, date of service, and total bill. The narrative: drafting the human story, how the injury affected the client's job, their parenting, or their hobbies. Liability proof: the police report, witness statements, and clear photos of the property damage. And special damages: lost wage verifications, such as W-2s or employer letters, and out-of-pocket receipts.

slides.title: Quality Control: The Final Scrub
slides.notes: Before a demand is sent, the Case Manager performs a final scrub to catch the common adjuster traps. Billing overlaps: make sure there is no double billing for the same date of service. Pre-existing conditions: highlight how the accident aggravated a previous injury, rather than trying to hide it. And balance verification: call every provider to get the final balance, so the demand amount is 100% accurate.

slides.title: Negotiating the First Call
slides.notes: For senior Case Managers who handle the first call with the adjuster, there are two things you need to know. The anchor technique: never apologize for a high demand, and stay firm on the value drivers. And note-taking: document every excuse the adjuster gives, such as low impact or delayed treatment. Those notes are the ammunition the attorney needs if the case goes to litigation.

slides.title: Demand: Best Practices
slides.notes: Here are the best practices for the demand. The 30-day rule: once a client reaches MMI, the demand must be out the door within 30 days. Photo impact: always lead the demand with the most graphic photo, of the property damage or the injury, to set the tone. The why factor: every medical bill in the demand needs a corresponding why, the reason that treatment was necessary for the client's recovery. And a pro tip to remember: a demand is not a request for money. It is a presentation of a debt owed. Treat the insurance company like a bank that has not paid its bill.

slides.title: Settlement Negotiations: The Pitch
slides.notes: Now we turn to settlement negotiations. In personal injury law, the demand letter is your opening move. If it looks like a template, the adjuster will treat it like one. Here is the negotiation battle map. First, create a net sheet: calculate the total medical liens, costs, and attorney fees. Anything below that total means the client receives nothing, and the aim is to maximize the net settlement. Second, identify the value drivers: list three facts that would scare a jury, such as the defendant was on his phone, or the client missed his daughter's wedding because of surgery. Third, anticipate the adjuster's response: name your top two weaknesses and prepare to justify them, ideally with documentation. And fourth, prepare the rebuttal, so the argument is ready before they bring it up. Adjusters protect insurance companies by undervaluing claims, so come prepared.

slides.title: The Valuation Baseline: The Set-Off
slides.notes: Next, the valuation baseline. In Bodily Injury settlements, PIP benefits are paid regardless of fault, and that complicates the claim against the at-fault party. Case Managers need to understand how these coverages relate, to make sure the client does not end up with zero. In most jurisdictions, the defendant's insurance carrier is entitled to a set-off, a credit, for payments made by PIP. The logic is that the law generally prevents double recovery. If PIP already paid the hospital ten thousand dollars, the defendant should not have to pay that same ten thousand dollars again. So the calculation is: the gross settlement value, minus the PIP paid amount, equals the defendant's remaining liability.

slides.title: The Valuation Baseline: PIP as a Valuation Baseline
slides.notes: BI adjusters use PIP payments to gauge how serious a claim is during the Demand Phase. Look first at the speed of exhaustion. If a client exhausts a ten thousand dollar PIP limit in 48 hours, as John Doe did with his ER and EMS bills, it signals a high-severity case. Then look at special damages. The total medical bills, the specials, are usually much higher than what PIP pays. Even though PIP covered ten thousand dollars, the Case Manager argues that the total value of the bills, forty-one thousand four hundred dollars in John's case, is the true anchor for the pain and suffering multiplier.

slides.title: The Valuation Baseline: The EMC and the Benefit Ceiling
slides.notes: As we saw in John Doe's file with Doctor Sarah Spine, the Emergency Medical Condition finding, the EMC, is a major negotiation lever. Without an EMC, many states cap PIP at two thousand five hundred dollars. That pushes more of the bills onto the BI settlement, often eating up the client's net recovery. With an EMC, the full ten thousand dollars is available. That is better for negotiations, because it lowers the amount of unpaid medical liens that have to be negotiated down at the end of the case.

slides.title: The Valuation Baseline: Subrogation vs. Non-Subrogation
slides.notes: This is the most critical technical detail in a BI negotiation: subrogation versus non-subrogation. Under non-subrogation, which is the common case, the PIP carrier cannot ask for its ten thousand dollars back from the BI settlement. That is a win for the client, because that money stays in their pocket, through the bills it already paid. Under subrogation, the PIP carrier places a lien on the BI settlement. The Case Manager must then negotiate with the PIP adjuster to reduce that lien, so the client keeps more of the final check.

slides.title: The Valuation Baseline: Strategic Exhaustion
slides.notes: A savvy Case Manager often wants PIP exhausted as quickly as possible on the hard costs, like the ER and imaging. Why? Once PIP is exhausted, the client can move to Letters of Protection, or LOPs, for later treatment like chiropractic care and physical therapy. And that gives you negotiation leverage. LOP providers are often more willing to reduce their bills at the end of a case than a hospital is. By spending the PIP money on the non-negotiable hospital bills, you preserve the BI settlement funds for the client. One tip: always verify the PIP ledger before you begin BI negotiations. If you tell an adjuster the specials are forty thousand dollars but forget that PIP already paid ten thousand of that, your credibility, and your demand, will be cut down instantly.

slides.title: Negotiations Initiated: The Battle
slides.notes: Negotiations officially begin once the demand packet is sent to the adjuster. Start with the soft lead, the first call. Confirm they received the demand and all the records. For example: Hi, I'm calling about the John Doe demand. I want to make sure you saw the MRI report on page 14 specifically. Then set the tone: state that the file is litigation ready. Next, the ask. If they have not made an offer, ask: Based on the clear liability and the forty thousand dollars in specials, what is your opening evaluation? And when the low-ball comes, never get angry. Use the professional pause. Count to five after they give a low number, then say: I'm struggling to see how that number accounts for the permanent nature of the injury. What data are you using to get there?

slides.title: The Bracketing Technique
slides.notes: When you are at one hundred thousand dollars and they are at thirty thousand, the gap feels impossible. Bracketing builds a bridge. First, propose the logic: We are seventy thousand dollars apart. If I can move my attorney into the eighty thousand range, can you get into the fifty thousand range? Second, check authority. If they say they don't have that much, ask: Who does? Because if we can't get into the fifties, we are wasting each other's time and should just file the complaint. Third, close the bracket. Once you are both between fifty and eighty thousand dollars, you negotiate the middle, for example, sixty-five thousand.

slides.title: Common Adjuster Stall Tactics
slides.notes: Adjusters use stalls to wear you down, so you accept a lower end-of-month settlement. Here are three, with the rebuttal for each. The stall: I'm waiting on my manager's authority. The rebuttal: Understood. I'll give you until Thursday at 4 PM. If I don't hear back, I've been instructed to send the file to our litigation department. The stall: We need more records from five years ago. The rebuttal: Those aren't relevant to this acute injury. However, if you want them, I expect an in-good-faith offer on the current undisputed injuries today. And the stall: The property damage was too low for this injury. The rebuttal: Physics doesn't work that way. Low-velocity impacts often cause high-torque injuries to the spine, and we have the MRI to prove it.

slides.title: Close the Deal: The Final-Final
slides.notes: The last two thousand five hundred dollars is often the hardest to get. Use the split the baby move: We are at forty-seven thousand, you're at forty-three. Let's meet at forty-five thousand, and I'll get the release signed within the hour. Before you hang up, confirm the terms. Is this for Bodily Injury only? Save property damage for later if it is not settled. Does it include all liens? And when will the check be mailed? Then create the paper trail. Immediately email the adjuster: Per our conversation, we have settled the John Doe matter for forty-five thousand dollars. Please send the release.

slides.title: The Never Rule
slides.notes: Finally, the never rule. Never apologize for a high demand. It is based on the client's suffering. Never bid against yourself. If you drop your price, the adjuster must raise theirs before you move again. And never accept that's all I have as the final answer on the first day. Every adjuster has a supervisor with a bigger checkbook.

slides.title: BI Settlement: The UM/UIM Safety Check
slides.notes: Now we reach the BI Settlement phase, and the UM/UIM safety check. If the at-fault driver has low or no insurance, you must tap into the client's own Uninsured or Underinsured Motorist coverage. That makes the subrogation waiver your green light. If you settle with the at-fault driver and sign their release without a waiver from your client's own insurer, you may destroy your client's right to collect UM/UIM benefits. So, first, send the 30-day letter: a formal notice to the UM carrier about the offer. Then secure the waiver document: a written Waiver of Subrogation from the UM carrier. It proves they have given up their right to sue the driver, which lets you settle the liability claim and proceed with the UM claim.

slides.title: BI Settlement: Key Laws & Doctrines
slides.notes: Before a settlement can be discussed, the file must be bulletproof, and that rests on three key laws and doctrines. The Made Whole Doctrine says a health insurer, the subrogated carrier, cannot claim from a settlement unless the client is fully compensated. It can help persuade lienholders to waive their claims when the settlement is small next to significant injuries. The Common Fund Doctrine requires lienholders to reduce their bill by the attorney's fee percentage, usually 33.3%. The logic: they should not get a free ride on the work the firm did to recover the money. And the Statute of Limitations is the death date for a case. Case Managers must track it religiously, because missing it is an automatic malpractice event.

slides.title: The Execution: The Release of All Claims
slides.notes: Now the execution. The Release of All Claims is the exit document, and the most critical document in the file. It is the contract that legally ends the dispute. In a release of Bodily Injury, make sure the client is not accidentally signing away a property damage or PIP claim that is still being negotiated separately. Know the non-admission of liability: standard releases state the insurer is paying to avoid further litigation, not because it admits its driver was at fault. And know the indemnity and hold harmless clause: the claimant, and their Case Manager and attorney, are responsible for paying all medical liens. If a hospital later sues the insurer over an unpaid bill, the claimant must indemnify, or pay back, the insurer for those costs.

slides.title: The Execution: The Settlement Disclosure Statement
slides.notes: The Settlement Disclosure Statement is the truth document. It is often required by state law or internal compliance, and it makes sure the claimant understands exactly what is happening. It states that the settlement is full and final: even if the claimant's back starts hurting again next year, they cannot come back for more money. And some states have a cooling-off period, a rescission period of a few business days, when the claimant can change their mind after signing. The Case Manager must track that date before cutting any checks.

slides.title: The Execution: Lien Payoff Letters
slides.notes: Lien payoff letters are the verification paperwork. A Case Manager cannot rely on a medical bill alone. You need a formal final demand, or payoff letter. If the claimant is 65+ or on SSDI, CMS, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, will issue a Medicare final demand. Be warned: it can take 60+ days to arrive, and the file must stay pended until it is in hand. And once a provider, like a chiropractor or a surgeon, is paid, obtain a signed letter stating the lien is satisfied. That satisfaction of lien keeps the provider from sending the client to collections later.

slides.title: The Execution: The Settlement Statement
slides.notes: The Settlement Statement is the net sheet: the ledger that breaks the settlement down from gross to net, and as a Case Manager you audit it for accuracy. Start with cost verification. Make sure every case cost, such as fifty dollars for a police report or two hundred dollars for medical records, is backed by a receipt. Then check the net to client, the final number the client actually receives. Your goal is to make sure that number is enough to cover any future medical needs discussed during the treatment phase.

slides.title: The Execution: The Dismissal
slides.notes: The dismissal is the court filing. If the case was already in litigation, meaning a lawsuit was filed, the settlement is not over until the court is notified. A dismissal with prejudice means the case is closed and cannot be refiled. A dismissal without prejudice, which is rare in settlements, allows the case to be refiled under specific conditions. So the Case Manager verifies that with prejudice is the language used, to make sure the file is fully closed.

slides.title: The Execution: W-9 and Key Post-Settlement Documents
slides.notes: Many insurance carriers will not issue a settlement check until they have a W-9 form from the law firm or the claimant. If the Case Manager does not request it the moment the verbal agreement is made, the check will be delayed by at least a week. Here is how the key post-settlement documents compare. The release is signed by the claimant, and it ends the right to sue. The final demand comes from the lienholder, such as Medicare or a hospital, and it states the exact amount needed to clear the debt. The W-9 is signed by the payee, the law firm or the claimant, for tax reporting to the IRS. And the stipulation to dismiss is signed by the attorneys, and it notifies the court that the case is over.

slides.title: Finalized Settlement: Administrative Document Control
slides.notes: Once the settlement is finalized and the paperwork is understood, the Case Manager enters the technical closing stage. Your mission is to move the file from settled to paid and archived, with total compliance. These are the boots-on-the-ground tasks, starting with administrative document control. The signature chase: send the Release of All Claims to the claimant by secure e-signature, like DocuSign, or schedule an in-person signing. Notary coordination: if the release needs a notary, which is common for high-value BI claims, verify that the notary's stamp is current and the ID matches the claimant exactly. And W-9 procurement: collect a W-9 from the claimant or the firm right away, so the carrier's accounting department does not flag the payment.

slides.title: Finalized Settlement: Final Lien Mitigation
slides.notes: The second set of closing tasks is final lien mitigation, the reduction. For provider negotiation, call the billing department of every lienholder. The script: The settlement was lower than expected. In the interest of global resolution, will you accept 50% of the balance as payment in full? Then update the ledger. Reflect every saving or reduction in the Settlement Statement right away, so the client can see their net recovery increasing. And for Medicare and Medicaid finalization, log into the MSPRP, the Medicare Secondary Payer Recovery Portal, and make sure the final demand matches your internal ledger.

slides.title: Thank You!
slides.notes: That brings us to the end of Day 2. Today we audited the file before the demand, built and presented the Bodily Injury demand, and negotiated and closed the settlement, all the way from settled to paid and archived. Review your notes on John Doe's file tonight, because we build on every one of these steps in the days ahead. Thank you.
